extraction.name: Natural Questions
extraction.description: A question answering dataset consisting of real anonymized, aggregated queries issued to the Google search engine, paired with Wikipedia pages from the top 5 search results. Annotators mark a long answer (typically a paragraph) and a short answer (one or more entities) if present on the page, or mark null if no answer is present.
extraction.creator: Tom Kwiatkowski, Jennimaria Palomaki, Olivia Redfield, Michael Collins, Ankur Parikh, Chris Alberti, Danielle Epstein, Illia Polosukhin, Jacob Devlin, Kenton Lee, Kristina Toutanova, Llion Jones, Matthew Kelcey, Ming-Wei Chang, Andrew M. Dai, Jakob Uszkoreit, Quoc Le, Slav Petrov
extraction.citeAs: Kwiatkowski, T., Palomaki, J., Redfield, O., Collins, M., Parikh, A., Alberti, C., Epstein, D., Polosukhin, I., Devlin, J., Lee, K., Toutanova, K., Jones, L., Kelcey, M., Chang, M.-W., Dai, A. M., Uszkoreit, J., Le, Q., & Petrov, S. (2019). Natural Questions: A Benchmark for Question Answering Research. Transactions of the Association for Computational Linguistics, 7, 453–466.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Questions consist of real anonymized, aggregated queries of 8 words or more issued to the Google search engine by multiple users in a short period of time. Queries are filtered using heuristic syntactic patterns and submitted back to the Google search engine to retain queries where a Wikipedia page appears in the top 5 search results. Human annotators are presented with the (question, Wikipedia page) pair to identify long and short answers.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: User-generated content data, Manual Human Curator
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: In total, annotators identify a long answer for 49% of the examples, and short answer spans or a yes/no answer for 36% of the examples. The authors consider the choice of whether or not to answer a question a core part of the QA task and deliberately do not discard the remaining 51% that have no answer labeled (NULL answers).
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Google search engine query logs and Wikipedia pages retrieved via Google search results.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Queries are filtered using heuristics based on length (8 words or more) and specific syntactic/lexical patterns (starting with who, when, where followed by specific verb forms, multiple entities, or categorical noun phrases). Hearst patterns are used to identify hypernyms, and part-of-speech tags and entities are detected using Google's Cloud NLP API. Only queries where a Wikipedia page is in the top 5 search results are kept.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotations are performed in three stages by a pool of annotators using a custom interface: 1) Question Identification (judging whether the question is good/fact-seeking or bad/ambiguous/opinion-seeking without seeing the Wikipedia page); 2) Long Answer Identification (selecting the earliest HTML bounding box such as paragraph, table, list item, or whole list containing enough information to infer the answer, or marking NULL); 3) Short Answer Identification (selecting entities within the long answer, flagging yes/no, or marking NULL). Average annotation time was 80 seconds per example.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Post-hoc evaluation was conducted using consensus judgments from four experts on non-null answers into three categories: Correct (C), Correct but debatable (Cd), and Wrong (W). Precision was estimated at 90% for long answers and 84% for short answers. Analysis of 25-way annotations on 302 examples evaluated human variability and agreement, showing that inter-annotator agreement correlates strongly with correctness, and that multiple acceptable answer spans often exist.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: 1 for training examples (307,373 items); 5 for development (7,830 items) and test (7,842 items) examples; 25 for an analysis subset of 302 examples.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: Focusing solely on Wikipedia as the evidence document source may introduce stylistic and topical biases compared to other web sources. Filtering out queries shorter than 8 words and excluding questions beginning with 'how to' also introduces bias in the query distribution.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: Excludes queries under 8 words and 'how to' procedural questions. Focuses only on Wikipedia pages rather than open web domains. Genuine ambiguity and acceptable variability exist across annotators regarding whether an answer is present or which text span constitutes the best answer.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Benchmarking, training, validation, and testing of open-domain and reading comprehension question answering systems and natural language understanding models.
